clue.text: The first Earl of! Oxford's way with doctors

parts.note: Robert Harley was created the first Earl of Oxford in 1711
a street is a way or road through a town

explanation.surface: A remark on how an eighteenth-century nobleman dealt with his physicians.
explanation.walkthrough: HARLEY STREET in London is lined with private medical consultants; the clue's 'way' is the street itself, not a manner.
explanation.definitionFit: London's Harley Street is famous as the home of private medical consultants and specialists.

clue.text: Dull murmur of a large party

parts.note: a hum is a low continuous murmur
a drum was an old name for a crowded evening party or assembly

explanation.surface: The tedious drone of conversation at a big gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: DRUM in the sense of a large fashionable party is an eighteenth- and nineteenth-century term, now found mainly in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Something humdrum is monotonous and lacking excitement, so it is dull.

clue.text: Rowdily gay or try to be perhaps

indicators.note: 'perhaps' says the letters of the two words could be arranged otherwise to form something new

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to be boisterously merry, or at least to make the effort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be perhaps' tells you to rearrange OR TRY. RORTY is British slang for lively, boisterous or rowdy in a cheerful way.
explanation.definitionFit: Rorty is old British slang for boisterous and jolly, so rowdy in its high spirits.

clue.text: He puts on a coat that's hard to outshine

definitions.text: He puts on a coat that's hard to outshine

parts.words: He puts on a coat that's hard to outshine
parts.note: the coat is not clothing but a hard glossy layer applied to metal or pottery, whose shine is difficult to beat

explanation.surface: A man dresses in a coat so smart nobody can upstage him.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'coat' is a coating of glassy vitreous finish, which is both hard and very shiny.
explanation.definitionFit: This craftsman applies vitreous glaze to metal or ceramics, a hard and glossy coating.

clue.text: Philistinism was fatal to this oratorio

definitions.text: Philistinism was fatal to this oratorio

parts.words: Philistinism was fatal to this oratorio
parts.note: Philistinism seems to mean lack of culture killing off a piece of music, but the literal Philistines killed the Israelite king who is the subject of a Handel oratorio

explanation.surface: An uncultured audience killed off a choral work.
explanation.walkthrough: Handel wrote an oratorio about the first king of Israel, who died fighting the Philistines at Mount Gilboa.
explanation.definitionFit: Handel's oratorio of 1739 is named after the first king of Israel, who fell in battle against the Philistines.

clue.text: That bauble a Manx cat has not

definitions.text: That bauble a Manx cat has not

parts.words: That bauble a Manx cat has not
parts.note: a Manx cat is tailless; the plant also called cat's-tail or cattail is a tall marsh plant whose brown spike resembles a mace or bauble

explanation.surface: A trinket that a particular breed of cat lacks.
explanation.walkthrough: A bauble was also a jester's mace or staff. The Manx cat, from the Isle of Man, has no tail, and this bulrush is also called cattail.
explanation.definitionFit: The bulrush plant is also known as cattail, a club-headed spike which the tailless Manx cat lacks.

clue.text: Snake that just fails to slip by

indicators.note: falling just short of the finish means the last letter of the word for passing is not reached

parts.note: time is said to elapse when it slips by

explanation.surface: A serpent that narrowly misses sneaking past someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'just fails' drops the final E of ELAPSE. Elaps is a genus of venomous snakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaps is the name of a genus of venomous snakes related to the coral snakes.

clue.text: Lots of punishment

definitions.meaning: floggings with a whip, a form of punishment

explanation.surface: Someone is getting a great deal of punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: Lashings is British for plenty, as in lashings of cream, and also floggings given as a punishment.

clue.text: Striking hangover

definitions.meaning: a heavy mallet used for striking
to overhang, as beetling brows or cliffs project

explanation.surface: A remarkable morning-after headache.
explanation.definitionFit: A beetle is a heavy wooden mallet for hammering, and something beetling juts out and overhangs.

clue.text: A vulgar madam married to a noble What's-his-name ?

parts.note: marm is a vulgar or colloquial pronunciation of ma'am, short for madam
a duke is a nobleman of the highest rank

explanation.surface: A coarse woman has married a peer whose name nobody can recall.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are in a different order from the clue: MARM, then A, then DUKE; 'married to' just joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's first name, here offered as a stand-in for an unnamed man, like 'so-and-so'.

clue.text: Yawning at the feast? Not pronouncedly

definitions.meaning: with the mouth wide open, as in a yawn
the love feast of the early Christians

explanation.surface: Someone yawning at a banquet, though not noticeably.
explanation.walkthrough: Both senses are spelt alike but said differently: the open-mouthed word rhymes with 'cape', the feast has three syllables, ah-ga-pay; 'Not pronouncedly' says so.
explanation.definitionFit: Open-mouthed as in a yawn, and the Greek-derived name of an early Christian communal love feast.

clue.text: A rehash of hers my poems are

indicators.note: a rehash reuses old material in a new form, so the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman's poems are just a rewrite of someone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A rehash of' tells you to rearrange the letters of HERS MY.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhymes are short verses, as in nursery rhymes, so poems.

clue.text: A very successful break

parts.note: reads as a lucky opportunity but describes a violent breaking blow, and is also the term for a show or song with huge success

explanation.surface: Someone has had a lucky opportunity.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'smash' is a break and a 'hit' is a blow; together they name a huge success.
explanation.definitionFit: A smash hit is an enormously popular record or show, and a smash is a breaking.

clue.text: Small round stone can spoil Common Market corn

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or damage
ble is French for wheat or corn, France being in the Common Market

explanation.surface: A pebble can damage the European Economic Community's grain.
explanation.walkthrough: The Common Market was the old name for the European Economic Community; its corn is taken in French, blé.
explanation.definitionFit: A marble is a small glass or stone ball used in children's games.

clue.text: Old soldiers a-hunting go?

definitions.meaning: ... were British soldiers of former times
fox-hunters ride out in scarlet coats

explanation.surface: Veterans setting off on a hunt.
explanation.definitionFit: British soldiers once wore scarlet tunics, and so do riders following hounds in a hunt.

clue.text: Science to get its own back has to take what no one else wants

definitions.text: take what no one else wants

parts.note: Sc is the abbreviation for science, as in BSc
to avenge is to get one's own back for a wrong

explanation.surface: Science seeking revenge must make do with leftovers.
explanation.definitionFit: To scavenge is to search through refuse and collect discarded things.

clue.text: Beautician's package?

parts.note: suggests a parcel from a beauty salon, but describes a small handbag holding cosmetics

explanation.surface: A parcel from a beauty specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: A small handbag for carrying make-up and a mirror, the tools of self-beautification.

clue.text: Word perfect ? Not one who acts her part

definitions.text: Word perfect ? Not one who acts her part

parts.words: Word perfect ? Not one who acts her part
parts.note: word-perfect usually describes an actor who knows the lines, but the character herself is famous for getting words wrong

explanation.surface: An actress who knows her lines, though not the one playing a certain role.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Malaprop, in Sheridan's play The Rivals, confuses similar-sounding words; whoever plays her must be word-perfect, but she is not.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheridan's comic character constantly misuses words, the source of the term malapropism.

clue.text: Dryad's soul-mate on the council ?

parts.note: a dryad is a tree nymph, so her ideal partner would be a tree-man, and the title is that of a senior member of a town council

explanation.surface: A tree nymph's true love has a seat in local government.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the title as ALDER MAN: a man of the alder tree, the ideal partner for a tree nymph.
explanation.definitionFit: An alderman is a senior councillor in a borough or city council.

clue.text: Pan's (hypothetical) tree, Archbishop

annotationWithheld.why: Pan's (hypothetical) tree, Archbishop: AN'S + ELM gives the archbishop, but nothing in the clue as held removes the P of Pan's, so the parse cannot be stated honestly.

clue.text: Othello's eyes were, to the melting mood

definitions.text: Othello's eyes were, to the melting mood

parts.words: Othello's eyes were, to the melting mood
parts.note: a quotation to complete from Othello's last speech, where he describes his eyes as not accustomed to weeping

explanation.surface: Othello's eyes, in his last speech, and their relation to tears.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello speaks of 'one whose subdued eyes, albeit ... to the melting mood, drop tears as fast as the Arabian trees their medicinal gum'.
explanation.definitionFit: Unaccustomed or not habituated, the word Othello uses for eyes not given to weeping.

clue.text: The lady's maid is so wooden

definitions.meaning: a servant who helps someone dress
a kitchen ... is a wooden piece of furniture with shelves

explanation.surface: A housemaid with a stiff, lifeless manner.
explanation.definitionFit: A dresser helps an actress or lady dress, and is also a sideboard made of timber.

clue.text: Bullish jobber ?

parts.note: sounds like a stock-exchange dealer expecting prices to rise, but describes a worker who looks after cattle

explanation.surface: A stock-exchange trader who is optimistic about prices.
explanation.walkthrough: A jobber was a dealer on the London Stock Exchange and a bull expects rises; but here the bulls are cattle and the job is tending livestock.
explanation.definitionFit: A stockman is a man employed to look after farm animals such as cattle.

clue.text: Jerry's broke

parts.note: Jerry is old British slang for a German, so the clue asks for the German-derived word for broken

explanation.surface: A man called Jerry has run out of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerry' looks like a man's name; it is wartime British slang for a German, and 'broke' means broken rather than penniless.
explanation.definitionFit: From German kaputt, meaning broken or finished.

clue.text: Horse's part in Othello's crime

definitions.meaning: the joint in a horse's hind leg, equivalent to the knee
Othello smothers Desdemona in her bed

explanation.surface: The role of a horse in Shakespeare's tragedy of murder.
explanation.definitionFit: The stifle is a hind-leg joint of a horse, and to smother, as Othello killed Desdemona.

clue.text: Evergreen Avenue, Leeds say ?

parts.note: a fir is an evergreen conifer
St, short for street, stands for a road or avenue

explanation.surface: An address: a tree-lined road in the Yorkshire city of Leeds.
explanation.walkthrough: Leeds is not the city: read it as 'leads', since whatever leads is in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To lead is to be in front of the rest, at the head of the field.

clue.text: Pope's great queen of little account in India

definitions.meaning: Alexander Pope addresses Queen Anne as 'great ..., whom three realms obey' in The Rape of the Lock
a coin of low value in India, a sixteenth of a rupee

explanation.surface: A grand queen in Pope's poetry who counted for little in India.
explanation.definitionFit: Pope's poetic name for Queen Anne, and a small former Indian coin worth one sixteenth of a rupee.

clue.text: Allow to be convalescent, but must rest

parts.note: to let is to allow
a convalescent patient is up, out of bed and recovering

explanation.surface: A recovering patient is allowed up, but must keep resting.
explanation.definitionFit: A let-up is a pause or easing off, a break from effort.

clue.text: Sound a bell — what Bellman does is fatal to trees

parts.note: to ring is to sound a bell
Bellman is a hound's name, in The Taming of the Shrew among others, and a dog barks

explanation.surface: A town crier rings his bell, and his work proves deadly to trees.
explanation.walkthrough: Bellman looks like the town crier with his bell, but it is the name of a hound. To ring-bark a tree is to cut a ring of bark from its trunk, killing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Ring-barking removes a band of bark round a trunk, cutting off the sap and killing the tree.

clue.text: She goes the pace, my girl — meaning my mate's

parts.note: a step is a single pace
my daughter is my girl

explanation.surface: A father complains that his daughter is fast, then says she is really his wife's.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is 'my mate's' daughter: the girl belongs to my spouse from an earlier marriage.
explanation.definitionFit: A spouse's daughter by a former marriage is related to you by marriage only.
